headline: UK inflation jumps to 3.5% in September, above forecasts, raising odds of a Bank of England rate rise

terms.meaning: Consumer Prices Index, the main measure of how fast prices rise.
The interest rate set by the Bank of England, which affects loans and savings.
Inflation leaving out volatile items such as food and energy.

levels.headline: UK inflation jumps to 3.5% in September, above forecasts, raising odds of a Bank of England rate rise
levels.body:
UK consumer price inflation rose to 3.5% in the 12 months to September 2026, up from 3.1% in August and above the 3.4% forecast by economists polled by Reuters, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).
Motor fuel prices were 29.8% higher than a year earlier. Core inflation, which strips out volatile items, climbed to 2.8% from 2.6%, and services inflation stood at 3.7%. Energy costs are the main pressure, linked to the US-Iran war and difficulty moving oil through the Strait of Hormuz. Britain is a net energy importer and so is exposed to such shocks.
The Bank of England's Bank Rate is 3.75%. In September its Monetary Policy Committee voted 6 to 3 to hold, with three members wanting a rise. Markets now expect the next decision, on 5 November, to lift the rate to 4%, with one estimate putting the chance at 98%. The next inflation figures are due on 18 November.
levels.why: Higher inflation squeezes household budgets and makes higher borrowing costs more likely.

levels.headline: UK inflation rises to 3.5% in September, ahead of expectations, as fuel costs surge
levels.body:
Consumer price inflation in the UK increased to 3.5% in the year to September, from 3.1% in August, the ONS said. Economists had expected 3.4%.
Petrol and diesel were 29.8% more expensive than a year earlier. Core inflation, which excludes items such as energy and food, rose to 2.8% from 2.6%, while services inflation was 3.7%. The rise is tied to higher oil prices caused by the US-Iran conflict and disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, and Britain imports much of its energy.
With Bank Rate at 3.75% after a 6 to 3 vote to hold in September, traders expect the Bank of England to raise it to 4% on 5 November. The next inflation release is on 18 November.
levels.why: It makes an interest rate rise more likely, which affects mortgages and savings.

levels.headline: UK inflation climbs to 3.5%, driven by the cost of fuel
levels.body:
The ONS reported that UK inflation rose to 3.5% in the year to September, up from 3.1% in August and higher than the 3.4% analysts expected.
Fuel was the biggest factor, with motor fuel prices up 29.8% on a year earlier. Underlying measures also moved up: core inflation, which leaves out energy and food, reached 2.8%, and services inflation was 3.7%. The rise is linked to the war involving the US and Iran, which has disrupted oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.
The Bank of England holds Bank Rate at 3.75%, but investors expect it to raise the rate to 4% on 5 November. Three of the nine policy-makers already voted for a rise in September.
levels.why: Rising prices and a likely rate rise would affect household finances.

levels.headline: UK inflation rises to 3.5% as fuel costs bite
levels.body:
UK inflation rose to 3.5% in September from 3.1% in August, the Office for National Statistics said, beating the 3.4% economists expected. Motor fuel was 29.8% dearer than a year ago.
Core inflation, which leaves out energy and food, edged up to 2.8%, and services inflation was 3.7%. Higher oil prices linked to the US-Iran war are the main cause.
The Bank of England holds Bank Rate at 3.75%, and markets expect a rise to 4% at its meeting on 5 November. Higher rates make mortgages and loans dearer but can help bring inflation down.
levels.why: Prices and borrowing costs both matter for household budgets.

levels.headline: UK inflation rises to 3.5% as petrol prices jump
levels.body:
Prices in the UK rose faster in September. The official figure for inflation, which measures how quickly prices go up, was 3.5% over the past year, compared with 3.1% in August. Experts had guessed 3.4%.
The main reason is fuel. Petrol and diesel cost almost 30% more than a year ago, partly because of the war involving the US and Iran, which has made oil harder to ship. Core inflation, which ignores food and energy because they jump around, also rose to 2.8%.
The Bank of England sets the interest rate, called Bank Rate, at 3.75%. Many investors now think it will raise it to 4% on 5 November, because higher rates can slow price rises. That would make loans and mortgages more expensive.
levels.why: Your weekly shop and travel costs more, and borrowing could get dearer too.

levels.headline: Prices are rising faster in the UK, mostly because of fuel
levels.body:
UK inflation, the rate at which prices rise, went up to 3.5% in the year to September. In August it was 3.1%. Most experts had expected a slightly smaller rise, at 3.4%.
Fuel is the big cause. Petrol and diesel now cost nearly 30% more than they did a year ago. Oil is more expensive because of the war involving the US and Iran, which has made it harder to move oil by ship. Britain buys a lot of its energy from abroad, so it feels these changes quickly.
The Bank of England decides the main interest rate, now 3.75%. People who trade money expect it to rise to 4% on 5 November. Raising rates is the Bank's way of slowing price rises, but it makes borrowing cost more.
levels.why: Higher prices and possibly higher mortgage costs affect most families.

levels.headline: Prices are going up faster in Britain
levels.body:
Official figures show prices rose 3.5% over the last year. A month earlier the figure was 3.1%. This is called inflation. It means your money buys a little less than before.
Petrol and diesel are the main reason. They cost nearly 30% more than a year ago. A war involving the US and Iran has made oil harder to ship, so it costs more. Britain buys much of its energy from other countries, so we feel the change.
The Bank of England sets an interest rate, which is the price of borrowing money. It is now 3.75%. Many people expect the Bank to raise it to 4% on 5 November to slow down rising prices. That would make loans and mortgages cost more.
levels.why: Things cost more, and borrowing money may soon cost more too.

levels.headline: Prices are rising faster, and petrol is a big reason
levels.body:
Inflation is how fast prices go up. In the UK it rose to 3.5% in the past year. Last month it was 3.1%. That means things like food and fuel cost a bit more than before.
The biggest change is petrol and diesel. They cost nearly 30% more than a year ago. There is a war involving the US and Iran. It makes oil harder to ship, so oil is dearer. Britain buys a lot of its energy from other countries.
The Bank of England controls the interest rate. This is the price of borrowing money. It is 3.75% now. Many people think the Bank will raise it to 4% on 5 November. When borrowing is dearer, people spend less, and that helps slow price rises.
levels.why: Your family may pay more for fuel, and loans may cost more.

levels.headline: Prices have gone up faster, mainly because petrol costs more
levels.body:
Prices in the UK are rising. This is called inflation. In the last year, prices went up by 3.5%. Last month it was 3.1%. So, on average, things cost a little more than before.
Petrol and diesel cost nearly a third more than last year. Oil is dearer because of a war between the US and Iran. Ships find it hard to carry oil. Britain buys lots of energy from other countries, so we pay more too.
The Bank of England is in charge of interest rates. An interest rate is the price you pay to borrow money. It is 3.75% now. The Bank will meet on 5 November. Many people think it will raise the rate to 4%. That helps slow prices, but it makes borrowing cost more.
levels.why: Shopping and petrol cost more, and borrowing may get dearer.

levels.headline: Why things in shops are costing a bit more
levels.body:
Imagine your favourite sweet cost 100 pence last year. Now it costs 103 or 104 pence. When lots of things get a little dearer like this, grown-ups call it inflation. This month it grew a bit faster.
The biggest reason is petrol. It costs a lot more than before, because of a war far away that makes oil hard to carry on ships. Cars and lorries need petrol, so many things become dearer.
There is a group of people at the Bank of England who look after money. They can raise something called the interest rate, which is like a fee for borrowing money. They think they might raise it soon. It is a bit like a teacher asking everyone to slow down in the playground.
levels.why: Grown-ups have to pay more for things, so they may have less to spend.

headline: S&P 500 closes down 0.52% at 7,623.68 as Dow drops more than 600 points on oil and AI spending worries

terms.meaning: An index tracking the share prices of 500 large US companies.
An index of shares, heavy with technology companies.
Cash a company has left after paying its running costs and investments.

levels.headline: S&P 500 closes down 0.52% at 7,623.68 as Dow drops more than 600 points on oil and AI spending worries
levels.body:
The S&P 500 closed down on the latest session CNBC reported, Thursday 22 October, falling 0.52% to 7,623.68. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 652.82 points, or 1.23%, to 52,215.16, and the Nasdaq Composite lost 0.21% to 25,955.34. A confirmed close for Friday 23 October was not available when this was written.
US oil prices topped $100 a barrel, with West Texas Intermediate futures up 3.8% to settle at $103.27, amid fears that the US-Iran conflict could flare up again. Investors also fretted about AI spending. Meta shares slid nearly 7% after its third-quarter results showed negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion and higher capital spending plans of $135 billion to $145 billion for the year.
Revenue at Meta rose 26% to $64.60 billion, beating forecasts, but the focus was on the cost of its artificial intelligence build-out.
levels.why: Share prices affect pensions and savings, and show how investors view oil and AI.

levels.headline: Wall Street falls: S&P 500 down 0.52%, Dow sheds 653 points as oil climbs and AI spending worries bite
levels.body:
The S&P 500 ended the latest reported session, Thursday 22 October, down 0.52% at 7,623.68. The Dow fell 1.23%, or 652.82 points, to 52,215.16, and the Nasdaq slipped 0.21% to 25,955.34. I could not confirm Friday's close.
Oil was a major driver. West Texas Intermediate settled at $103.27 a barrel, up 3.8%, on fears of renewed conflict between the US and Iran. Concern over heavy AI spending added to the gloom after Meta fell nearly 7%.
Meta's quarterly revenue beat expectations at $64.60 billion, but free cash flow was negative $2.12 billion and it raised its spending floor for the year to between $135 billion and $145 billion.
levels.why: Falling markets can reduce the value of pensions and shift borrowing costs.

levels.headline: US shares fall as oil tops $100 and investors worry about AI costs
levels.body:
US shares fell in the latest session reported, on Thursday 22 October. The S&P 500, which tracks 500 big companies, closed down 0.52% at 7,623.68. The Dow dropped 1.23% to 52,215.16 and the Nasdaq edged down 0.21% to 25,955.34. We could not confirm the Friday close.
Oil prices rose above $100 a barrel because investors fear the US-Iran conflict could flare up again. Investors were also anxious about how much firms are spending on artificial intelligence. Meta shares fell nearly 7%.
Meta made more money than expected, but it spent so heavily on AI that it burned through cash, and it plans to spend even more this year.
levels.why: It shows how fears about war and technology can move global markets.

levels.headline: Wall Street slides as oil climbs above $100 and AI worries grow
levels.body:
US shares fell in the latest session we could confirm, on Thursday 22 October. The S&P 500 lost 0.52% to close at 7,623.68, the Dow fell 1.23% to 52,215.16 and the Nasdaq eased 0.21% to 25,955.34. A Friday close was not confirmed.
US crude settled at $103.27 a barrel, up 3.8%, on fears that conflict between the US and Iran could return. Meta shares dropped nearly 7% after it reported negative free cash flow and higher spending plans.
Investors are weighing the cost of heavy AI investment against the returns it may bring.
levels.why: Falling shares can affect pensions and investor confidence.

levels.headline: US stock market ends lower as oil jumps and AI worries grow
levels.body:
The main US share index, the S&P 500, fell 0.52% on the latest day reported, Thursday 22 October, closing at 7,623.68. The Dow, which tracks 30 large firms, lost 1.23% and closed at 52,215.16. The Nasdaq, full of tech companies, slipped 0.21% to 25,955.34. We could not confirm Friday's result.
Oil went above $100 a barrel because people worry that fighting between the US and Iran could start again. Higher oil prices push up costs for many businesses. Investors were also nervous about how much tech firms spend on AI. Meta's shares fell nearly 7%.
Meta earned more than expected, but it spent so much on AI that it ran out of spare cash for the quarter.
levels.why: Share prices can affect pensions, and dearer oil can push up prices at the pump.

levels.headline: US shares fall because oil is dear and people worry about AI spending
levels.body:
US share prices went down on Thursday 22 October, the last day we could confirm. The S&P 500 is a list of 500 big US companies. It fell 0.52% to 7,623.68. The Dow, another group of big companies, fell 1.23% to 52,215.16. The Nasdaq, which has many tech firms, fell 0.21% to 25,955.34.
Oil cost more than $100 a barrel. People worry that the US and Iran may fight again, and that would make oil even dearer. Investors also worried about companies spending huge amounts on AI. Meta shares dropped nearly 7%.
Meta earned more money than experts guessed. But it is spending so much on AI that it had no spare cash left over.
levels.why: Many pensions are invested in shares, so big falls can matter to ordinary people.

levels.headline: Share prices fell in the US because oil costs more and AI is costly
levels.body:
On Thursday 22 October, share prices in the US went down. A share is a small piece of a company. The S&P 500 index, which follows 500 big companies, fell by about half of one percent. The Dow fell by about one and a quarter percent. The Nasdaq fell a little.
Oil cost more than $100 a barrel. People fear that the US and Iran may fight again. If oil costs more, lots of things cost more. People were also worried about AI. Meta spent so much money on AI that its share price fell almost 7%.
We could not check what happened on Friday, so these are the latest numbers we are sure about.
levels.why: When shares fall, savings and pensions that hold them can be worth less.

levels.headline: Share prices dropped in America because of oil and AI worries
levels.body:
On Thursday 22 October, the price of shares in big American companies went down. A share is a tiny slice of a company. The S&P 500 is a list of 500 big companies. Its value fell by about half of one percent. Another list, called the Dow, fell by more than one percent.
Oil cost more than $100 a barrel. There is a war between the US and Iran, and people fear it may get worse. Oil is used to make petrol, so it matters to everyone. Also, a big company called Meta is spending huge amounts on AI, and people worried about that.
We could not check Friday's numbers, so we are telling you about Thursday.
levels.why: Money that people save for the future is often held in shares.

levels.headline: Prices of shares in America fell today
levels.body:
Shares are tiny pieces of companies. People buy them hoping they will be worth more later. On Thursday 22 October, the price of shares in many big American companies went down. The main list, called the S&P 500, went down by about half of one percent.
One reason was oil. Oil is what makes petrol for cars. It cost more than $100 for a barrel, and people worry that a war may make it dearer still. Another reason was a company called Meta. It is spending lots and lots of money on AI computers, and people were worried.
We could not find the numbers for Friday, so this is the last day we are sure about.
levels.why: Many families save for the future in shares, so these ups and downs matter.

levels.headline: Why shares went down, told like a playground story
levels.body:
Think of the school playground where children swap stickers. The price of a sticker goes up and down depending on how many people want it. Shares in companies work a bit like that. On Thursday 22 October, shares in America were worth a little less than before.
One worry was oil, which gives us petrol for cars. It got dearer because of a faraway war. Another worry was that one big company, Meta, is spending huge amounts on new computer brains called AI. Some people thought it was too much.
We could not find out what happened on Friday, so we are telling you about Thursday.
levels.why: Grown-ups save money in shares, so when prices drop they may feel worried.

headline: UK borrowed £24.5 billion in September, £1.9 billion above the OBR forecast, ONS says

terms.meaning: The gap between what the government spends and what it takes in, in a given period.
The Office for Budget Responsibility, the official forecaster of the public finances.
The government's accounting year, which runs from April to March.

levels.headline: UK borrowed £24.5 billion in September, £1.9 billion above the OBR forecast, ONS says
levels.body:
UK public sector net borrowing was £24.5 billion in September 2026, according to the Office for National Statistics. That was £1.8 billion, or 7.7%, more than in September 2025 and £1.9 billion above the forecast by the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR). It was the second-highest September on record, behind 2020.
In the financial year to September, borrowing was £97.8 billion. That is £4.4 billion, or 4.3%, less than a year earlier, but £6.0 billion above the OBR's forecast. The current budget deficit was £15.8 billion in September and £64.0 billion so far this year, also above forecast.
Trading Economics reports that public sector net debt passed £3 trillion for the first time. The next release is on 20 November. A budget is due on 28 October.
levels.why: Borrowing above forecast puts pressure on tax and spending decisions in the coming budget.

levels.headline: UK borrowing in September higher than forecast at £24.5 billion
levels.body:
The government borrowed £24.5 billion in September 2026, the ONS reported. That was £1.8 billion more than a year earlier and £1.9 billion more than the OBR had forecast. Only September 2020 saw higher borrowing for that month.
Over the financial year so far, borrowing totals £97.8 billion, which is £4.4 billion lower than at this point last year but £6.0 billion above the OBR's forecast. The current budget deficit reached £15.8 billion in September.
Public sector net debt has passed £3 trillion for the first time, according to Trading Economics. The figures come a week before the budget on 28 October.
levels.why: It tightens the room the government has to cut taxes or raise spending.

levels.headline: UK government borrowing was higher than expected in September
levels.body:
The UK government borrowed £24.5 billion in September, the ONS said. That was more than a year earlier and £1.9 billion more than the official forecaster, the OBR, had expected. It was the second-highest September since records began, behind 2020.
So far this financial year, which began in April, borrowing is £97.8 billion. That is lower than last year, but still £6.0 billion above what the OBR predicted. Total public debt has gone past £3 trillion for the first time, according to Trading Economics.
These numbers arrive ahead of the budget on 28 October, when the government sets out its tax and spending plans.
levels.why: The government has less spare money, which can mean tough budget choices.

levels.headline: UK borrowing overshoots forecast in September
levels.body:
The government borrowed £24.5 billion in September, £1.9 billion more than the OBR forecast and the second-highest September on record, the ONS said.
Borrowing for the financial year so far is £97.8 billion, below last year's level but £6.0 billion above the OBR's forecast. Public sector net debt has passed £3 trillion for the first time, according to Trading Economics.
The figures come days before the budget on 28 October, where the Chancellor will set out tax and spending plans.
levels.why: It limits what the government can afford to do in the budget.

levels.headline: The UK government borrowed more than expected in September
levels.body:
The government borrowed £24.5 billion in September. Borrowing means spending more than it collects in taxes. The official forecaster, the OBR, had expected about £1.9 billion less. Only September 2020 was worse.
Since April, the government has borrowed £97.8 billion. That is a little less than this time last year, but £6.0 billion more than the OBR forecast. The total owed by the public sector, called debt, has passed £3 trillion for the first time.
A budget is due on 28 October. That is when the Chancellor explains how the government will raise and spend money. Higher borrowing makes those choices harder.
levels.why: Debt must be paid back with interest, which affects taxes and public services.

levels.headline: The government borrowed more than experts expected in September
levels.body:
The government spends money on things like schools, hospitals and roads. It gets money from taxes. When it spends more than it gets, it borrows the difference. In September it borrowed £24.5 billion. Experts had expected about £1.9 billion less.
Since April it has borrowed £97.8 billion. That is a bit less than last year but more than forecast. The total the public sector owes, called debt, has gone above £3 trillion for the first time. That is a huge number.
A budget is due on 28 October. In a budget, the government says how it will collect taxes and spend money. Borrowing more than planned can make those decisions harder.
levels.why: Money owed has to be paid back with interest, so it affects taxes and services.

levels.headline: The UK government borrowed more money than expected
levels.body:
Each month the government spends money on schools, hospitals and roads. It collects taxes to pay for this. If it needs more, it borrows. In September it borrowed £24.5 billion, which is more than experts expected.
Since April it has borrowed £97.8 billion. That is a little less than last year, but more than the experts' guess. All the money the public sector owes, called debt, is now over £3 trillion. That is the first time.
On 28 October there will be a budget. This is when the government explains its plans for taxes and spending. Borrowing more than planned makes the plan harder to make.
levels.why: Borrowed money must be paid back, so it affects taxes and public services.

levels.headline: The government borrowed more money than it planned
levels.body:
A government is a bit like a big family. It gets money from taxes. It spends money on schools, hospitals and roads. If it spends more than it gets, it has to borrow. In September, it borrowed £24.5 billion. That was more than experts thought.
Since April it has borrowed £97.8 billion. The total it owes, called debt, is now more than £3 trillion. That is the first time it has been so big. Debt has to be paid back, and the government pays extra, called interest, for borrowing.
On 28 October there will be a budget. That is when the government shares its plan for taxes and spending.
levels.why: What the government owes affects the taxes people pay and the services they get.

levels.headline: The government borrowed more than it hoped
levels.body:
Imagine your class has a money jar for trips. Each month, some money goes in and some goes out. If more goes out than comes in, you must borrow some. The government did this in September. It borrowed £24.5 billion, which was more than people guessed.
Since April it has borrowed £97.8 billion. All the money it owes added together is now more than £3 trillion. That is a number so big it is hard to picture. Borrowed money has to be paid back, with a little extra.
On 28 October, the government will explain its plans for the money jar.
levels.why: The money the government owes is paid back using the taxes people pay.

levels.headline: Why the government's money jar is running low
levels.body:
Think of pocket money. If you spend more than you get each week, you must borrow from someone. The government does this too, but with far bigger numbers. In September it borrowed £24.5 billion, which was more than grown-ups had guessed.
Over the whole year so far it has borrowed £97.8 billion. All the money it owes is now over £3 trillion. Money that is borrowed must be paid back, and a little extra is paid for the loan.
Soon, on 28 October, the government will tell everyone how it plans to look after its money jar.
levels.why: Grown-ups pay taxes to help pay back what the government has borrowed.

headline: UK government approves Jackdaw North Sea gas field, which could raise domestic gas output by 6% at peak

terms.meaning: A fresh official decision made after an earlier one was struck down.
Greenhouse gases released when the oil or gas is eventually burned.
Cutting greenhouse gas emissions to balance what is removed from the air.

levels.headline: UK government approves Jackdaw North Sea gas field, which could raise domestic gas output by 6% at peak
levels.body:
The UK government has approved the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea, with supplies to British homes and businesses possible from the end of this month. The decision is a re-determination after the Court of Session ruled the earlier consent unlawful because downstream emissions had not been taken into account.
Officials say Jackdaw would lift domestic gas production by around 6% at peak, with a field life of up to 11 years. The government accepts the project will not end UK dependence on gas imports or change prices. Ministers frame it as an energy security measure.
Green Party leader Zack Polanski called it "climate vandalism", while industry groups welcomed the decision. The government has yet to decide whether to approve Rosebank, thought to hold the UK's largest untapped oil reserves.
levels.why: It shows how the government is balancing energy security against climate goals.

levels.headline: UK gives go-ahead to Jackdaw gas field after court ruling forced a new decision
levels.body:
The government has granted consent for the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea, which could supply gas by the end of October. The decision was remade after the Court of Session found the original consent unlawful because it did not consider downstream emissions.
Peak output would raise UK gas production by about 6%, and the field could last up to 11 years. The government concedes it will neither remove import dependence nor affect prices.
Zack Polanski, the Green leader, called the move "climate vandalism", and industry bodies welcomed it. A decision on the Rosebank oil field is still outstanding.
levels.why: The decision tests how far energy security can sit alongside climate commitments.

levels.headline: Government approves controversial North Sea gas field
levels.body:
The UK government has approved drilling at the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea. Gas could reach homes and businesses as soon as the end of the month. The government had to decide again after a Scottish court ruled the first approval unlawful, because it had ignored the emissions released when the gas is burned.
The government says Jackdaw would raise UK gas production by about 6% at its peak and run for up to 11 years. It admits this will not end the need for imported gas or bring prices down.
Green Party leader Zack Polanski called the decision "climate vandalism". Industry groups welcomed it. No decision has yet been made on Rosebank, a big undeveloped oil field.
levels.why: It affects how Britain gets its energy and how it meets climate goals.

levels.headline: Ministers approve Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea
levels.body:
The government has approved the Jackdaw gas field, with gas possibly flowing by the end of the month. The decision was remade after a Scottish court found the first consent unlawful because it ignored the emissions from burning the gas.
Officials expect Jackdaw to raise UK gas output by about 6% at its peak, over a life of up to 11 years, though they accept it will not end imports or change prices.
Green leader Zack Polanski called it "climate vandalism", while industry welcomed the move. A decision on Rosebank is still to come.
levels.why: It balances energy supply against climate goals.

levels.headline: UK says yes to a new North Sea gas field
levels.body:
The government has approved a gas field in the North Sea called Jackdaw. Gas from it could be sent to British homes and businesses as soon as the end of October. The government had to decide again because a court in Scotland said the first decision was against the law. It had not counted the pollution made when the gas is burned.
Jackdaw would add about 6% to the gas made in the UK at its busiest, and could work for up to 11 years. The government says it will not stop Britain buying gas from abroad, and will not change what people pay.
The Green Party leader, Zack Polanski, called it "climate vandalism". Industry groups were pleased. A decision on another field, Rosebank, has not been made.
levels.why: It is about how Britain gets its energy while trying to cut pollution.

levels.headline: The UK approves a gas field under the North Sea
levels.body:
The government has said yes to a gas field called Jackdaw under the North Sea. Gas from it could reach homes as soon as the end of the month. The government had to decide again. A court in Scotland said the first yes was against the rules, because it did not think about the pollution made when gas is burned.
Jackdaw would add about 6% to the gas made in the UK at its busiest. It could work for up to 11 years. The government says Britain will still need to buy gas from other countries, and bills will not change because of it.
The leader of the Green Party called the decision "climate vandalism", meaning it harms the climate. Companies that work with oil and gas were pleased.
levels.why: People disagree about whether to use more gas now or move faster to cleaner energy.

levels.headline: The government says yes to a new gas field
levels.body:
The government has agreed that a gas field called Jackdaw can start work in the North Sea. Gas from it could come to homes in a few weeks. The government had to think again because a court said its first decision was not allowed. It had not counted the pollution that comes when gas is burned.
The field would add a small amount, about 6%, to the gas the UK makes. It could run for up to 11 years. The government says we will still buy gas from other countries, and prices will not change.
Some people are angry. The leader of the Green Party said it harms the climate. Companies that work with gas are happy. The government has not yet decided about another field, called Rosebank.
levels.why: It shows leaders choosing between energy at home and protecting the climate.

levels.headline: A new gas field gets the green light
levels.body:
The government has said a gas field called Jackdaw can open in the sea near Britain. Gas is used to cook food and warm homes. This gas could reach people very soon. The government had to decide twice. A court said the first time was wrong, because it forgot to count the pollution made when gas is burned.
The field would make a bit more of the gas we use. It could work for up to 11 years. We will still need to buy gas from other countries, and it will not make bills smaller.
Some people say it hurts the planet. Others say it keeps our energy safe. The government has not yet decided about another field called Rosebank.
levels.why: People are asking how we can keep warm and also look after the planet.

levels.headline: Britain says yes to a gas field
levels.body:
Gas helps us cook our dinner and keep our homes warm. Some of it comes from under the sea near Britain. The government has said that a new place to get gas, called Jackdaw, can open. A court said the first yes was wrong, so the government had to think again.
The new gas field would help a little. It would add a bit to the gas Britain makes. But we would still buy gas from other countries. Bills would not get smaller.
Some people feel worried that burning gas hurts the planet. Others feel it is important to have our own gas. It is hard to choose, a bit like choosing between two games at playtime.
levels.why: Grown-ups must decide how to keep homes warm and care for the planet.

levels.headline: A new gas field for Britain, and some people are cross
levels.body:
Imagine our house needs a fire to keep warm, and we can burn wood from our own garden or buy wood from far away. Britain is a bit like this with gas. The government has said yes to a new gas field under the sea, which is like using a bit more wood from our own garden.
A court said the first yes was a mistake, so the grown-ups had to decide again. Some people say burning gas hurts the planet, like making the air dirty. Others say it keeps us warm and safe.
Grown-ups are still talking about it, and another field is still waiting for a decision.
levels.why: Grown-ups have to balance keeping homes warm with looking after the planet.

headline: UK to send RAF Typhoon jets on defensive missions to help protect Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks

terms.meaning: A flight that protects an area by intercepting attacking aircraft or missiles.
An Iran-backed armed group that controls much of Yemen.
A large military transport aircraft.

levels.headline: UK to send RAF Typhoon jets on defensive missions to help protect Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks
levels.body:
The UK announced on 20 October that RAF Typhoon fighter jets will fly defensive counter-air missions to protect Saudi cities and critical national infrastructure from aerial attack by Yemen's Houthis. The Ministry of Defence says the jets will not carry out offensive strikes on the Houthis.
The package also includes an RAF A400M transport aircraft to move defence materiel within Saudi Arabia and UK military advisers to support Saudi staff officers. It builds on a Voyager air-to-air refuelling aircraft sent about a month ago at Riyadh's request.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting condemned the Houthi attacks, which have included strikes on Riyadh airport that caused deaths and flight cancellations, and on Saudi Aramco facilities. France has also pledged a strictly defensive approach.
levels.why: It deepens UK involvement in a conflict that is already pushing up oil prices.

levels.headline: UK Typhoons to fly defensive missions over Saudi Arabia as Houthi attacks escalate
levels.body:
The government has said RAF Typhoons will fly defensive counter-air missions to protect Saudi cities and key infrastructure from Houthi attacks. The Ministry of Defence stresses the jets will not strike the Houthis.
An A400M transport aircraft and military advisers will support Saudi forces, adding to a Voyager refuelling aircraft already provided at Riyadh's request.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting condemned Houthi attacks on Riyadh airport and Saudi Aramco sites. The UK says Saudi Arabia and Yemen have the right to defend themselves, and France has pledged defensive support too.
levels.why: It marks a bigger UK military role in the Gulf at a time of high oil prices.

levels.headline: Britain sends fighter jets to help defend Saudi Arabia
levels.body:
The UK has announced that RAF Typhoon fighter jets will help protect Saudi Arabia from attacks by the Houthis, an armed group in Yemen. The Ministry of Defence says the flights will be defensive only, meaning they will try to stop incoming attacks rather than attack the Houthis.
Britain will also send a transport aircraft and military advisers, in addition to a refuelling plane sent about a month ago at Saudi Arabia's request.
The Defence Secretary, Wes Streeting, condemned recent Houthi attacks, which hit Riyadh airport and oil company Aramco's sites. France has also promised a defensive approach.
levels.why: It shows how conflict in the Middle East draws in the UK and affects energy prices.

levels.headline: RAF Typhoons to help defend Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks
levels.body:
The UK said on 20 October that RAF Typhoon jets will fly defensive missions to protect Saudi cities and key sites from Houthi aerial attacks. The Ministry of Defence says they will not strike the Houthis.
An A400M transport aircraft and military advisers will also be sent, adding to a refuelling aircraft supplied a month ago.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting condemned the attacks, which have hit Riyadh airport and Aramco facilities. France has promised a strictly defensive approach too.
levels.why: It widens the UK's role in a conflict that is lifting oil prices.

levels.headline: UK fighter jets will help protect Saudi cities
levels.body:
The UK says RAF Typhoon fighter jets will fly to help protect Saudi Arabia from attacks by the Houthis, an armed group in Yemen. The Ministry of Defence says the jets will only defend. They will try to stop missiles and drones, and they will not attack the Houthis.
Britain will also send a large transport plane and military advisers to help Saudi officers. A refuelling plane was sent about a month ago because Saudi Arabia asked for it.
The Defence Secretary, Wes Streeting, said the Houthi attacks were wrong. They hit Riyadh airport and sites owned by the oil company Aramco, and people were killed. France has also promised to help in a defensive way.
levels.why: The UK is getting more involved in a far-away conflict that affects oil prices.

levels.headline: Britain will send fighter jets to protect Saudi Arabia
levels.body:
The UK has said it will send RAF Typhoon fighter jets to Saudi Arabia. Their job is to defend. They will help stop attacks on Saudi cities by a group called the Houthis, who are based in Yemen. The Ministry of Defence says the jets will not attack the Houthis.
Britain is also sending a big cargo plane and military advisers to help Saudi officers. A plane that refuels other aircraft in the sky was sent a month ago because Saudi Arabia asked.
The Defence Secretary, Wes Streeting, said the attacks were wrong. Houthi attacks hit an airport in Riyadh, and people died. They also hit sites owned by the oil company Aramco.
levels.why: What happens in the Middle East can change oil prices and what we pay for petrol.

levels.headline: The UK will send jets to help keep Saudi Arabia safe
levels.body:
The UK has said it will send fighter jets, called Typhoons, to Saudi Arabia. A group called the Houthis, who live in Yemen, has been attacking Saudi cities. The jets will only defend. That means they will try to stop attacks. They will not attack the Houthis.
The UK is also sending a big cargo plane and some military helpers who give advice. A month ago it sent a plane that gives fuel to other planes in the air.
The Defence Secretary, Wes Streeting, said the attacks were wrong. People died when an airport in Riyadh was hit. France has also said it will help, but only to defend.
levels.why: Fighting far away can make oil dearer and may affect life in Britain.

levels.headline: Britain is sending jets to help protect Saudi Arabia
levels.body:
Saudi Arabia is a country in the Middle East. A group called the Houthis has been sending missiles and drones at its cities. Britain has now said it will send some of its fighter jets to help. The jets will only protect. They will not attack anyone.
Britain is also sending a big cargo plane and some helpers from the army. They will give advice to Saudi officers. A plane that gives fuel to other planes has already been sent.
The people in charge in Britain said the attacks were wrong, because people were hurt and an airport was hit. France has also said it will help to defend.
levels.why: Trouble in the Middle East can make petrol and gas cost more.

levels.headline: Britain sends helpers to protect another country
levels.body:
Imagine a boy in your school is being bothered by older children. Some friends decide to stand near him to protect him, but not to fight. Something like this is happening in the Middle East. A group called the Houthis keeps sending missiles at cities in Saudi Arabia.
Britain has said it will send fighter jets to help protect the cities. The jets will only protect. They will not attack. Britain is also sending a cargo plane and some advisers.
The leaders of Britain think the attacks are wrong. France has also said it will help in the same way.
levels.why: What happens far away can affect the price of petrol at home.

levels.headline: Friends who stand guard
levels.body:
Imagine a playground where some big children keep throwing balls at a smaller child. Some other children say, we will stand in front and catch the balls, but we will not throw any back. This is a bit like what Britain is doing for Saudi Arabia.
A group called the Houthis keeps sending missiles and drones at Saudi cities. Britain is sending special planes that can fly fast. They will try to stop the missiles. They will not attack.
Britain is also sending a big carrying plane and some helpers. France has said it will help too.
levels.why: Grown-ups worry because fighting far away can change the price of petrol.

headline: France imposes partial curfews after cost-of-living protests turn to looting, with soldiers to be deployed for Saturday's demonstrations

terms.meaning: A rule that people must stay indoors during set hours.
The French military force that patrols public places for security.
Special legal powers a government can use in a crisis.

levels.headline: France imposes partial curfews after cost-of-living protests turn to looting, with soldiers to be deployed for Saturday's demonstrations
levels.body:
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu ordered localised, partial curfews after cost-of-living protests on 17 October turned into looting and clashes. Paris introduced overnight curfews around Place de la République and Les Halles, and Lille and Nice also brought in restrictions. Lecornu said the curfews contributed to a calm night.
Protest organisers said 550,000 to 800,000 people took part, far above the roughly 200,000 Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez expected. Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin reported about 2,500 people in police custody. For Saturday 24 October, soldiers from the Sentinelle force and elite police and gendarmerie units will be deployed.
Lecornu said a state of emergency had not been ruled out but that targeted curfews were better suited. Unions have called for further action on 5 November.
levels.why: Unrest over living costs is testing the French government and Europe's second-largest economy.

levels.headline: French government orders curfews and deploys troops after weekend of rioting over living costs
levels.body:
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has ordered local, partial curfews after protests over the cost of living on 17 October descended into looting. Paris, Lille and Nice have all brought in restrictions, and Lecornu said they helped bring a calm night.
Turnout was far larger than the authorities expected, at 550,000 to 800,000 according to organisers against the 200,000 forecast by the interior minister. About 2,500 people were taken into custody, Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said.
Soldiers from the Sentinelle force and elite police units will be on the streets for Saturday's protests. A state of emergency has not been ruled out, and unions have called for action on 5 November.
levels.why: It raises pressure on President Macron over living costs and public order.

levels.headline: France brings in curfews after protests over living costs turn violent
levels.body:
France has brought in partial curfews in several cities after a weekend of protests over the cost of living turned into rioting and looting. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu ordered the measures, and Paris, Lille and Nice have all introduced restrictions.
Organisers said between 550,000 and 800,000 people joined the protests, much higher than the 200,000 the interior minister had expected. About 2,500 people were detained, according to Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin.
Soldiers and special police units will be deployed for further protests on Saturday. The government has said it is not ruling out a state of emergency, and unions have called for more action on 5 November.
levels.why: The unrest shows how strongly rising living costs are affecting people in Europe.

levels.headline: France brings in curfews and troops after cost-of-living riots
levels.body:
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has ordered partial curfews after cost-of-living protests on 17 October turned to looting. Paris, Lille and Nice have restrictions, and Lecornu said they brought a calm night.
About 2,500 people were taken into custody, Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said. Soldiers from the Sentinelle force and elite police units will be deployed for Saturday's protests.
A state of emergency has not been ruled out, and unions have called for more action on 5 November.
levels.why: It tests the French government as living costs bite.

levels.headline: France sets curfews after riots, and troops will be on the streets
levels.body:
Large protests about the cost of living took place across France on 17 October. Some turned violent, with shops looted. The French Prime Minister, Sébastien Lecornu, has now ordered curfews in some places. A curfew means people must stay off the streets at certain times, usually at night. Paris, Lille and Nice have all brought them in.
Many more people came to the protests than the government expected. Around 2,500 people were arrested. On Saturday, soldiers and special police will be on the streets in case there is more trouble.
The government says it may use stronger emergency powers if needed. Trade unions have called for more action on 5 November.
levels.why: People in France are angry about prices, and this affects the whole of Europe.

levels.headline: France puts curfews in place after riots
levels.body:
On 17 October, huge protests about high prices took place in France. The protests turned violent in some places, and shops were looted. The Prime Minister, Sébastien Lecornu, has ordered curfews. A curfew is a rule that people must stay inside at set times, such as at night. Paris, Lille and Nice have them.
Far more people turned up than the government had expected. About 2,500 people were taken in by the police. Soldiers and special police will be out on Saturday to keep order.
The government says it has not ruled out stronger powers, called a state of emergency. Trade unions want more protests on 5 November.
levels.why: Rising prices are making many people in Europe angry and worried.

levels.headline: France brings in night curfews after riots over prices
levels.body:
Many people in France are upset because things cost too much. On 17 October, there were huge protests. Some turned into riots and shops were robbed. The Prime Minister has now said some cities can have curfews. A curfew means people must stay at home at certain times, such as late at night.
Many more people came to the protests than the government thought. About 2,500 people were arrested. On Saturday, soldiers and police will be out on the streets to keep people safe.
The government says it could use special emergency powers if it has to. Trade unions want more protests on 5 November.
levels.why: Money worries can make people angry, and this is happening in a big European country.

levels.headline: Riots in France over high prices
levels.body:
Many people in France say that things cost too much. They went out on the streets to protest. This was on 17 October. A lot of people came. Most were peaceful, but in some places there was trouble. Some shops were broken into and robbed.
The Prime Minister said some cities can have curfews. This is a rule that people must stay at home late at night. It helped, and one night was calm. About 2,500 people were arrested.
On Saturday, soldiers and police will be out in the streets to keep people safe. Unions say there will be more protests on 5 November.
levels.why: People get upset when money is tight, and leaders must try to keep everyone safe.

levels.headline: Trouble on the streets of France
levels.body:
In France, many people are upset because things in shops cost so much. They marched in the streets in big crowds. In some places, the crowds became angry and shops were damaged. Some things were stolen.
The leader of the government, the Prime Minister, said some towns could have a rule called a curfew. It means people must stay at home late at night, so the streets are quiet and safe. It helped, and the next night was calm.
Soldiers and police will be out on Saturday, to help keep people safe. The grown-ups are still talking about how to make things better.
levels.why: When people cannot afford things, they can become very upset.

levels.headline: When lots of people are upset in France
levels.body:
Imagine everyone in the school canteen was cross because the lunch prices went up. They might all stand up and shout. Now imagine this happening in a whole country. In France, many grown-ups are upset because things cost so much, and they marched in the streets.
Most people wanted to be heard, but in some places there was damage. The leaders said some towns must be quiet at night. This is called a curfew. It is a bit like a bedtime rule for a whole town.
Soldiers and police will be out on Saturday to keep people safe. Grown-ups are still talking about how to help.
levels.why: Leaders must listen when many people are upset, and keep everyone safe.

headline: Putin meets US envoy Witkoff as Zelenskyy backs freezing the front line, but fighting continues

terms.meaning: An agreement to stop fighting, even if no final peace deal is reached.
The line where the two armies face each other.
Promises from other countries to help protect a nation if it is attacked again.

levels.headline: Putin meets US envoy Witkoff as Zelenskyy backs freezing the front line, but fighting continues
levels.body:
US envoy Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin for more than three hours in St Petersburg on 21 October. Russia freed detained American teacher Stephen Hubbard during the visit. Witkoff called the talks "constructive" but said "important work" remained, while the Kremlin said his proposals offered "little of real value".
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said halting the fighting along the current front line is the most realistic route to ending the war. He said Ukraine could accept a ceasefire there without recognising Russian sovereignty over occupied territory, and wants security guarantees from the US and European allies.
Fighting went on: Russia and Ukraine traded overnight attacks, with seven killed on the Ukrainian side. Moscow is in principle willing to resume three-way talks, potentially in mid-November after the US midterm elections.
levels.why: The talks could decide whether the war in Europe moves towards a ceasefire.

levels.headline: Witkoff holds three-hour talks with Putin; Zelenskyy proposes a ceasefire on current lines
levels.body:
Steve Witkoff, the US envoy, met Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg for over three hours on 21 October. Russia released US citizen Stephen Hubbard. Witkoff described the talks as constructive, but the Kremlin dismissed his proposals as offering little of real value.
Volodymyr Zelenskyy said freezing the front line is the most realistic first step towards a ceasefire, without Ukraine recognising Russian control of occupied land. He wants security guarantees from Washington and European partners.
Overnight strikes continued, killing seven in Ukraine. The Kremlin says it is open in principle to trilateral talks, possibly in mid-November after the US midterms.
levels.why: Any ceasefire in Ukraine would reshape European security and energy markets.

levels.headline: US envoy meets Putin while Zelenskyy backs a ceasefire along the current front line
levels.body:
US envoy Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin for more than three hours in St Petersburg. Russia freed an American teacher, Stephen Hubbard, during the visit. Witkoff called the talks constructive, but the Kremlin said his proposals offered little of real value.
Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said stopping the fighting where the armies now stand is the most realistic way to end the war. Ukraine would not accept that Russia owns the land it has taken, and it wants security guarantees from the US and Europe.
Attacks continued overnight, and seven people were killed in Ukraine. Russia says it could rejoin three-way talks, perhaps in mid-November.
levels.why: It shows how far apart the sides remain, even as talks continue.

levels.headline: Putin and Witkoff talk for three hours as Zelenskyy backs a ceasefire on current lines
levels.body:
US envoy Steve Witkoff met Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg on 21 October, and Russia freed American Stephen Hubbard. Witkoff called the talks constructive, while the Kremlin said his proposals offered little of real value.
Volodymyr Zelenskyy said freezing the front line is the most realistic first step, without recognising Russian control of occupied land, and he wants security guarantees.
Attacks continued overnight, killing seven in Ukraine. Moscow may rejoin trilateral talks in mid-November.
levels.why: A ceasefire would change security across Europe.

levels.headline: A US envoy met Putin, and Ukraine's leader asks for a pause in fighting
levels.body:
A US envoy, Steve Witkoff, spent more than three hours talking with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg. Russia let an American teacher, Stephen Hubbard, go free. Witkoff said the talks were helpful. The Kremlin said his ideas were not worth much.
Ukraine's leader, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said the best next step is to stop fighting where the armies are now. This is called freezing the front line. He says Ukraine would not agree that the land Russia took belongs to Russia. He also wants other countries to promise to help protect Ukraine.
The fighting has not stopped. Seven people were killed in new attacks. Russia says it might join talks again in mid-November.
levels.why: Peace in Ukraine would affect safety, energy prices and the economy across Europe.

levels.headline: Putin talks to a US envoy, and Ukraine asks for a pause in fighting
levels.body:
A man called Steve Witkoff works for the US president. He travelled to Russia and talked with President Putin for more than three hours. Russia also let an American teacher, Stephen Hubbard, come home. Mr Witkoff said the talks were helpful. Russia said his ideas were not worth much.
Ukraine's leader, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wants the fighting to stop where the armies are now. This is called a ceasefire. He says Ukraine will not say that the land Russia took belongs to Russia. He wants other countries to promise to keep Ukraine safe.
The fighting has not stopped. Seven people were killed in new attacks. Russia says it may talk again in mid-November.
levels.why: The war has hurt many people, and it affects prices and safety in Europe.

levels.headline: A meeting about ending the war in Ukraine
levels.body:
A man called Steve Witkoff, who works for the US, went to Russia. He talked with its leader, Vladimir Putin, for more than three hours. Russia let an American teacher go free at the same time. Mr Witkoff said the talks were helpful. Russia said his ideas were not worth much.
The leader of Ukraine, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wants the fighting to stop now, where the armies are. That is called a ceasefire. He does not want to say that land Russia took belongs to Russia. He wants other countries to promise to help keep Ukraine safe.
Sadly, the fighting goes on. Seven people died in new attacks. Russia says it might talk again in mid-November.
levels.why: A ceasefire would save lives and help Europe feel safer.

levels.headline: People are talking about stopping the war in Ukraine
levels.body:
There is a war between Russia and Ukraine. A man from the US, called Steve Witkoff, went to Russia to talk with its leader, Vladimir Putin. They talked for more than three hours. Russia also let a teacher from America go home. Mr Witkoff said the talks were useful.
Ukraine's leader wants the fighting to stop where the armies are now. That is called a ceasefire. He wants other countries to promise to keep his country safe.
But the fighting has not stopped. Seven people died in new attacks. Russia says it may talk again in mid-November.
levels.why: Many people have been hurt by the war, and everyone hopes it can end.

levels.headline: Grown-ups talk about ending a war
levels.body:
Two countries, Russia and Ukraine, have been fighting for a long time. A man from America went to Russia to talk to its leader about stopping the fighting. They talked for more than three hours. A teacher from America who was in trouble was set free at the same time.
The leader of Ukraine says the best next step is to stop fighting right where the armies are now. He also wants other countries to promise to keep his country safe.
But the fighting has not stopped, and some people were hurt. Russia says it may talk again in mid-November.
levels.why: Everybody hopes the fighting will stop so people are safe.

levels.headline: Trying to stop a big quarrel
levels.body:
Imagine two groups of children are in a big quarrel in the playground. A teacher from another class goes to talk to one group's leader. They talk for a long time. But the quarrel does not stop right away. This is a bit like what is happening between Russia and Ukraine.
The leader of Ukraine says, let us stop where we are now. Then we can talk. He also wants friends to promise to help keep his country safe.
People are still being hurt, which is very sad. Grown-ups hope to talk again in the middle of November.
levels.why: Everyone hopes the quarrel will end soon, so that people are safe.

headline: Eurozone growth slows in October as France contracts, with the ECB expected to hold on 29 October

terms.meaning: Purchasing Managers' Index, a survey where a reading above 50 means growth.
The ECB's key interest rate, paid on banks' deposits with it.
The European Central Bank, which sets interest rates for the euro area.

levels.headline: Eurozone growth slows in October as France contracts, with the ECB expected to hold on 29 October
levels.body:
The eurozone composite PMI fell to 51.9 in October from 53.1 in September, a three-and-a-half-year high, and below the 52.7 economists had expected. Manufacturing dipped to 52.4. France's composite reading dropped to 48.4 from 51.1, well below the 50.5 forecast. Any reading under 50 indicates contraction.
Eurozone inflation reached 3.8% in September, a three-year high, driven mostly by energy costs linked to the Iran war. The European Central Bank raised its deposit rate to 2.5% on 10 September, its second rise of the year.
Traders expect the ECB to hold rates at its meeting on 29 October and raise them again in December. The euro has weakened to around $1.111, its lowest since mid-May 2025, which can add to import costs.
levels.why: Slower growth with high inflation makes life harder for the ECB and for households.

levels.headline: Eurozone activity cools as French economy shrinks; ECB seen on hold before a December rise
levels.body:
The eurozone composite PMI slipped to 51.9 in October from 53.1, missing the 52.7 forecast. Manufacturing eased to 52.4, and France fell into contraction territory at 48.4, from 51.1.
Inflation in the euro area was 3.8% in September, a three-year high, largely due to energy costs tied to the Iran war. The ECB lifted its deposit rate to 2.5% on 10 September.
Markets expect no change at the 29 October meeting and another rise in December. The euro is near $1.111, its weakest since mid-May 2025.
levels.why: It shows the euro area facing weaker growth and higher prices at once.

levels.headline: Eurozone economy slows in October as France slips into contraction
levels.body:
A survey of businesses across the eurozone suggests growth slowed in October. The composite PMI fell to 51.9 from 53.1 in September. A reading above 50 means growth, so the economy is still growing, but more slowly than forecast. In France the reading fell to 48.4, which signals shrinking activity.
Prices are also rising quickly. Eurozone inflation hit 3.8% in September, a three-year high, mainly because of more expensive energy linked to the war involving Iran. The European Central Bank raised its main rate to 2.5% in September.
Traders think the bank will wait on 29 October and raise rates again in December. The euro has also fallen to about $1.111.
levels.why: Weaker growth and dearer energy affect jobs, prices and mortgage costs in Europe.

levels.headline: Eurozone growth slows as France contracts
levels.body:
The eurozone composite PMI fell to 51.9 in October from 53.1, below the 52.7 forecast, and France dropped to 48.4, which signals contraction.
Inflation reached 3.8% in September, a three-year high driven by energy costs linked to the Iran war. The ECB raised its deposit rate to 2.5% on 10 September.
Traders expect it to hold on 29 October and raise again in December. The euro has slid to about $1.111.
levels.why: Weaker growth with high prices squeezes households.

levels.headline: Europe's economy is slowing, and France is shrinking
levels.body:
A survey of businesses across the countries that use the euro shows the economy grew more slowly in October. The survey gives a score, where above 50 means growth. The eurozone score fell to 51.9 from 53.1. In France it fell to 48.4, which means business activity there is shrinking.
Prices are going up quickly too. Inflation reached 3.8% in September, the highest in three years. Energy is the main cause, because of the war involving Iran. The European Central Bank raised its main interest rate to 2.5% in September.
Traders expect the bank to wait on 29 October and raise rates again in December. The euro has lost value and is worth about $1.111.
levels.why: Slow growth and high prices at the same time are hard for families and governments.

levels.headline: Europe's economy is growing more slowly, and France's is shrinking
levels.body:
Businesses across the euro countries were asked how things are going. The answers give a score, and above 50 means the economy is growing. In October the score fell to 51.9 from 53.1. In France it fell to 48.4, which means shrinking.
Prices are also going up. Inflation reached 3.8% in September, the highest for three years. Energy is more expensive because of the war involving Iran. The European Central Bank, which sets the interest rate for the euro countries, raised the rate to 2.5% in September.
People who trade money expect it to wait on 29 October and raise it again in December. The euro has also lost value against the dollar.
levels.why: When growth slows but prices rise, it is harder for families to manage.

levels.headline: Europe's money news: slower growth and higher prices
levels.body:
Many countries in Europe use the same money, the euro. Businesses there were asked how things are going. The answers show the economy is still growing, but more slowly than before. In France, the score fell low enough to show the economy is shrinking.
Prices keep going up as well. They rose 3.8% in the last year, the biggest rise for three years. Energy costs more because of a war involving Iran. The bank that looks after the euro, called the ECB, raised its interest rate to 2.5% in September.
People think the bank will wait on 29 October, then raise the rate again in December. The euro is also worth less than before.
levels.why: Slower growth and high prices mean families have to be careful with money.

levels.headline: Europe's economy is slowing down
levels.body:
Lots of countries in Europe use the same money, called the euro. Businesses there said that things are growing more slowly now. In France, things have started to shrink. That means companies are making and selling a bit less than before.
Prices have also gone up quickly, by 3.8% in a year. Energy costs more because of a war involving Iran. The bank for the euro, called the ECB, charges 2.5% to borrow money. It raised that rate in September to slow price rises.
People think the bank will wait on 29 October, then raise the rate again in December.
levels.why: It can affect jobs, prices and holidays for people in Europe.

levels.headline: Europe's money is growing more slowly
levels.body:
Many countries in Europe use the same coins and notes, called the euro. Companies there have said business is slowing down. In France, companies are making and selling less than before. That is not good for shops, workers or families.
Things in shops are also costing more. This is because energy, like gas for heating, costs more. A war far away has made this happen. A big bank, called the ECB, has made it dearer to borrow money. It did this to try to slow down rising prices.
The bank may wait in October and raise the cost again in December.
levels.why: Families may find life harder when money is tight and prices are high.

levels.headline: Why Europe's money news feels a bit gloomy
levels.body:
Think of a bike race. At first the riders go fast. Then some get tired and slow down. That is what is happening to the economy in Europe. It is still moving forward, but more slowly. In France, the riders have almost stopped.
At the same time, shop prices are rising because energy is dearer. A big bank in Europe, called the ECB, can make borrowing cost more. It did this in September, to slow price rises.
Grown-ups think it may wait in October and do it again in December.
levels.why: Slow growth and dear shopping make it harder for families to plan.
